questions.prompt: You clap and hear the echo from a building 0.5 s later. Sound travels at 344 m/s. How far away is the building?
What is the minimum distance from a wall needed to hear a distinct echo in air (v = 344 m/s)?
questions.explain: 344 × 0.1 = 34.4 m there and back, so 17.2 m each way.

feedback.3: That’s the total there-and-back distance; halve it.

questions.prompt: A girl stands 170 m from a cliff and claps. How long until she hears the echo? (v = 340 m/s)

questions.explain: Hard, smooth surfaces reflect; soft, porous ones absorb.

options: The lingering of sound caused by many overlapping reflections
A change in pitch of a moving source
questions.explain: Repeated reflections in an enclosed space make sound persist.

questions.prompt: Why are the ceilings of concert halls often curved?
options: To make the sound travel faster
To reflect sound evenly towards the audience
To stop echoes by trapping sound
questions.explain: Curved surfaces direct reflected sound to all parts of the hall.

questions.prompt: A bat squeaks and hears the echo from a moth 0.02 s later. How far away is the moth? (v = 340 m/s)
A new school auditorium has so much reverberation that speeches are hard to hear. Explain the cause and suggest two solutions.
questions.modelAnswer: Sound reflects many times off the hard walls, floor and ceiling, and the reflections overlap, so each syllable lingers and blurs into the next. Adding soft, sound-absorbing materials (curtains, carpets, upholstered seats, acoustic panels on walls or ceiling) reduces reflections. Placing absorbing panels at the back wall and using fewer bare hard surfaces also helps.
rubric: Solution 2 with absorbing material or design
questions.explain: Criterion D: acoustics in building design.
